sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. Hypothetical burst lengths and budgets introduced in an exercise are not measured workload traces, and labels assigned by the generator are not empirical student difficulty measurements.

These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

function.description:
Deterministic single-processor RR or STCF scheduling with independent, single-burst processes and no I/O. Times are integer abstract time units. Initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free. RR boundary=before/after orders arrivals exactly at a slice end before/after the unfinished process is requeued; earlier waiting processes keep their position. during_switch=tail appends switch-time arrivals to the queue; before_preempted inserts them immediately before the just-preempted process if it is still queued, otherwise at the tail. The next process is selected before switching, and arrivals through the switch end are enqueued before it starts. early_finish_free waives the next different-process switch cost only if the previous process completed in less than a full quantum. Same-process continuation is free. STCF supports zero switch cost only and chooses (remaining time, id), including id-based preemption on equal remaining times. Id comparison is Unicode lexicographic order. switch_count counts adjacent different-process transitions, including free early-finish transitions, but excludes initial/idle dispatch. makespan is final completion measured from time zero, including initial and intermediate idle intervals. Consecutive run intervals for the same process without an intervening switch/idle interval are merged.

function.description:
Deterministic single-processor RR or STCF scheduling with independent, single-burst processes and no I/O. Times are integer abstract time units. Initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free. RR boundary=before/after orders arrivals exactly at a slice end before/after the unfinished process is requeued; earlier waiting processes keep their position. during_switch=tail appends switch-time arrivals to the queue; before_preempted inserts them immediately before the just-preempted process if it is still queued, otherwise at the tail. The next process is selected before switching, and arrivals through the switch end are enqueued before it starts. early_finish_free waives the next different-process switch cost only if the previous process completed in less than a full quantum. Same-process continuation is free. STCF supports zero switch cost only and chooses (remaining time, id), including id-based preemption on equal remaining times. Id comparison is Unicode lexicographic order. switch_count counts adjacent different-process transitions, including free early-finish transitions, but excludes initial/idle dispatch. makespan is final completion measured from time zero, including initial and intermediate idle intervals. Consecutive run intervals for the same process without an intervening switch/idle interval are merged.

brief.learning_goal: Given a small fixed workload with stated arrival times and CPU service lengths, specify a reproducible execution timeline under declared switching, tie-break and slice-boundary conventions, compare competing policies (e.g., Round Robin at two slice sizes versus a shortest-job policy) on mean response time, mean turnaround time, switch count and switching overhead, and defend a policy choice against a stated objective and at least one concrete constraint while acknowledging that one metric alone does not establish a best policy.
requirements: Use a finite workload of at most four explicit scenarios, each listing arrival times, CPU service lengths, time-slice lengths and only the allowed metrics (mean response, mean turnaround, makespan, overhead, switch count).

State every convention needed for a reproducible timeline: whether switching overhead applies and when, the tie-break rule, and whether a job arriving exactly at a slice boundary is enqueued before or after the preempted job.

Require per-job first-run and completion times plus computed mean response and mean turnaround for at least two competing policies, and require the stated switching budget or overhead accounting to be applied consistently.

Require a justified policy recommendation that names the objective and at least one explicit constraint (maximum response time, switching budget, or fairness), and that explains how a policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on a different metric.

Forbid relying on unstated future job lengths: the response must say how execution lengths are known, or treat a policy that needs them as inapplicable; keep the whole argument within the supplied scheduling model and notes.

sections.heading: Scheduling metrics and conventions
sections.text: Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

expected_steps: Order execution and switching intervals using the stated rules.
Compute process metrics and exact averages from first starts and completions.
Check service conservation and the requested state or constraint judgments.

questions.stem:
Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

Processes (arrival, burst):

A: (0, 1)

B: (1, 10)

C: (2, 10)

D: (3, 10)

S1: RR; quantum q=2, different-process switching cost=1. Arrivals before a slice end are queued first; arrivals exactly at the slice end are queued before the unfinished process is requeued, while existing waiters keep their order. Select the next process before switching; arrivals during switching, including its end, are appended to the queue tail before the selected process starts. Waive the next different-process switching cost only when the previous process completed in its just-ended run slice and that slice was strictly shorter than a full quantum.

S2: RR; quantum q=5, different-process switching cost=1. Arrivals before a slice end are queued first; arrivals exactly at the slice end are queued before the unfinished process is requeued, while existing waiters keep their order. Select the next process before switching; arrivals during switching, including its end, are appended to the queue tail before the selected process starts. Waive the next different-process switching cost only when the previous process completed in its just-ended run slice and that slice was strictly shorter than a full quantum.

S3: STCF; switching cost is 0. At each integer time choose the arrived unfinished process with the smallest (remaining service, lexicographic process ID); a smaller ID can preempt the current process even when remaining service is equal.

For every scenario, give the complete timeline; each process’s first start, response, completion and turnaround; mean response, mean turnaround, switch count, total switching overhead and makespan. Use exact fractions for averages.

Among scenarios satisfying mean turnaround time <= 25 and process switch count <= 8 and total switching overhead <= 6, minimize mean response time. Show every constraint check, report all tied optima, or state that no scenario is feasible.

questions.focus: Recommending a scheduling policy under explicit response-time, switching-overhead and fairness constraints, with a reproducible timeline.
questions.learning_goal: Given a small fixed workload with stated arrival times and CPU service lengths, specify a reproducible execution timeline under declared switching, tie-break and slice-boundary conventions, compare competing policies (e.g., Round Robin at two slice sizes versus a shortest-job policy) on mean response time, mean turnaround time, switch count and switching overhead, and defend a policy choice against a stated objective and at least one concrete constraint while acknowledging that one metric alone does not establish a best policy.
requirements: Use a finite workload of at most four explicit scenarios, each listing arrival times, CPU service lengths, time-slice lengths and only the allowed metrics (mean response, mean turnaround, makespan, overhead, switch count).

State every convention needed for a reproducible timeline: whether switching overhead applies and when, the tie-break rule, and whether a job arriving exactly at a slice boundary is enqueued before or after the preempted job.

Require per-job first-run and completion times plus computed mean response and mean turnaround for at least two competing policies, and require the stated switching budget or overhead accounting to be applied consistently.

Require a justified policy recommendation that names the objective and at least one explicit constraint (maximum response time, switching budget, or fairness), and that explains how a policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on a different metric.

Forbid relying on unstated future job lengths: the response must say how execution lengths are known, or treat a policy that needs them as inapplicable; keep the whole argument within the supplied scheduling model and notes.
